paragraphs: Here our inquiries are brought to an awe-inspiring halt. But why should I hide my views? Considering the attributes of God, I believe that whatever punishment may follow will serve, like the pain of disease, to show the malignancy of vice for the purpose of reform. Positive punishment seems so contrary to the nature of God, as we discover it in all his works and in our own reason, that I could sooner believe the Deity paid no attention to men’s conduct than that he punished without the benevolent aim of reforming them.

Merely to suppose that an all-wise and all-powerful Being, as good as he is great, would create a creature, foreseeing that after fifty or sixty years of feverish existence it would be plunged into never-ending misery — is blasphemy. On what will the worm feed that is never to die? On folly, on ignorance, you say — I would blush with indignation at drawing the natural conclusion, could I set it down here, and would wish to withdraw myself from under the wing of my God! On such a supposition — I speak with reverence — he would be a consuming fire. We would wish, though in vain, to flee from his presence when fear had swallowed up love and darkness had wrapped all his counsels.

I know that many devout people boast of submitting blindly to the Will of God, as to an arbitrary sceptre or rod, on the same principle on which the Indians worship the devil. In other words, like people in the ordinary affairs of life, they pay homage to power and cringe beneath the foot that can crush them. Rational religion, by contrast, is submission to the will of a being so perfectly wise that all he wills must be directed by the proper motive — must be reasonable.

And if this is how we respect God, can we believe the mysterious hints that insult his laws? Can we believe, even if it stared us in the face, that he would work a miracle to authorize confusion by sanctioning an error? Yet we must either accept these impious conclusions, or treat with contempt every promise to restore health to a diseased body by supernatural means, or to foretell events that only God can foresee.
SECTION 13.2.
Another example of that feminine weakness of character, often produced by a narrow education, is a romantic turn of mind that has very properly been called SENTIMENTAL.

Women, made subject to their sensations by ignorance, and taught to look for happiness only in love, refine upon sensual feelings and adopt metaphysical notions about that passion, which lead them shamefully to neglect the duties of life; and often, in the midst of these sublime refinements, they plunge into actual vice.

These are the women who are entertained by the fantasies of stupid novelists, who, knowing little of human nature, work up stale tales and describe meretricious scenes, all peddled in a sentimental jargon, and all equally apt to corrupt the taste and to draw the heart away from its daily duties. I do not mention the understanding, because, never having been exercised, its dormant energies lie idle, like the hidden particles of fire that are supposed to pervade all matter.

In fact, women, denied all political privileges and not allowed, as married women, a civil existence except in criminal cases, naturally have their attention drawn away from the interest of the whole community to that of its tiny parts, although the private duty of any member of society must be very imperfectly performed when it is not connected with the general good. The great business of a woman’s life is to please; and, since political and civil oppression keeps her from entering into more important concerns, feelings become events, and reflection deepens what it should have erased, and would have erased, if the understanding had been allowed a wider range.

But, confined to trivial occupations, they naturally absorb the opinions inspired by the only kind of reading suited to interest an innocent, frivolous mind. Unable to grasp anything great, is it surprising that they find reading history a very dry task, and treatises addressed to the understanding unbearably tedious and almost unintelligible? So they are bound to depend on the novelist for amusement. Yet when I protest against novels, I mean novels as compared with works that exercise the understanding and regulate the imagination. For I think any kind of reading better than leaving a blank still a blank, because the mind must be enlarged to some degree and gain a little strength from a slight exercise of its thinking powers; besides, even works addressed only to the imagination lift the reader a little above the gross gratification of appetites to which the mind has not lent a shade of delicacy.

This remark comes from experience; for I have known several capable housewives, and one in particular, who was a very good woman — as good as so narrow a mind would allow her to be — and who made sure that her daughters (three of them) never saw a novel. Being a woman of fortune and fashion, she had various masters come to teach them, and a sort of servant-governess to watch their every step. From their masters they learned what tables, chairs, etc. were called in French and Italian; but since the few books put in their way were either far beyond their capacities or devotional, they acquired neither ideas nor feelings, and, when they were not forced to repeat WORDS, spent their time dressing, quarrelling with one another, or talking secretly with their maids, until they were brought into society as marriageable.

Their mother, a widow, was meanwhile busy keeping up her connections, as she called a large circle of acquaintance, so that her girls would not lack a proper introduction into the great world. And these young ladies, with minds vulgar in every sense of the word and with spoiled tempers, entered life puffed up with ideas of their own importance, and looking down with contempt on those who could not compete with them in dress and show.

As for love, nature, or their nurses, had taken care to teach them the physical meaning of the word; and since they had few topics of conversation and fewer refinements of feeling, when they spoke freely, talking of matrimony, they voiced their gross wishes in none too delicate phrases.

Could these girls have been harmed by reading novels? I almost forgot one shade in the character of one of them: she affected a simplicity bordering on silliness, and with a simper would utter the most immodest remarks and questions, whose full meaning she had learned while shut away from the world and afraid to speak in the presence of her mother, who ruled with a high hand. They were all educated, as their mother prided herself, in a most exemplary way, and read their chapters and psalms before breakfast, never touching a silly novel.

This is only one instance; but I remember many other women who, not having been led step by step to proper studies, nor allowed to choose for themselves, have indeed remained overgrown children, or have picked up, by mixing in the world, a little of what is called common sense — that is, a clear way of seeing ordinary events as isolated occurrences; but anything deserving the name of intellect, the power of forming general or abstract ideas, or even intermediate ones, was out of the question. Their minds were inert, and when they were not stirred by objects of the senses and by occupations of that kind, they were low-spirited, and would cry or go to sleep.

When, therefore, I advise my sex not to read such flimsy works, it is to persuade them to read something better; for I agree with a shrewd man who, having a daughter and a niece in his care, followed a very different plan with each.

The niece, who had considerable abilities, had been allowed to read at random before she was placed under his guardianship. He tried to lead her, and did lead her, to history and moral essays; but his daughter, whom a doting, weak mother had indulged, and who was consequently averse to anything like application, he allowed to read novels; and he used to justify his conduct by saying that if she ever acquired a taste for reading them, he would have some foundation to build on, and that mistaken opinions were better than none at all.

In fact, the female mind has been so completely neglected that knowledge could be acquired only from this muddy source, until, through reading novels, some women of superior talents learned to despise them.

The best way, I believe, to correct an excessive liking for novels is to ridicule them — not indiscriminately, for then it would have little effect; but if a judicious person with some sense of humour were to read several to a young girl, and show her, both by tone of voice and by apt comparisons with moving incidents and heroic characters in history, how foolishly and absurdly they caricatured human nature, sound opinions might take the place of romantic sentiments.

In one respect, however, most people of both sexes are alike, and show an equal lack of taste and modesty. Ignorant women, forced to be chaste to preserve their reputation, let their imagination revel in the unnatural and meretricious scenes sketched by the novel writers of the day, dismissing as insipid the sober dignity and matronly grace of history,* while men carry the same corrupted taste into life, and flee from the unaffected charms of virtue and the grave respectability of good sense to seek amusement with the wanton.

(*Footnote. I am not referring here to that superiority of mind which leads to the creation of ideal beauty, when life, surveyed with a penetrating eye, appears a tragicomedy in which little can be seen to satisfy the heart without the help of imagination.)

Besides, reading novels makes women, and especially ladies of fashion, very fond of using strong expressions and superlatives in conversation; and although the dissipated, artificial life they lead keeps them from cherishing any strong, legitimate passion, the language of passion in affected tones slips endlessly from their glib tongues, and every trifle sets off those phosphorescent bursts that merely mimic in the dark the flame of passion.
